artboards.title: Before — The day as it ships today (1240)
The days that are not a busy Tuesday
The day sheet — A4, one page

annotations.text:
The day, designed from the four jobs it actually does: closing tonight, looking back, settling an argument, and judging whether it was a good day.
The screen answers them in that order — was it good, is it properly recorded, what happened, what was decided.
Read left to right: what ships today, then the console, then the states.

2,620px of one column on a 1,440px screen.
Four figures with nothing to measure them against. Every row carries a 112px cell that six of the eight lists leave empty. "Ran out" — the most consequential line of a trading day — is a footnote. Thirty-one till entries are one sentence under the fold.

The console. The verdict is the top 260px: four figures, each against the middle of the last five Tuesdays.
Under it, money and the shelf in the main column; how the day closed, the working behind the comparison, and the day's work in the rail. The morning's meeting and what became of each move closes the page.
One accent: Print the day, because on a day already closed and counted that is the only thing left to do.

The same screen at 16:52 on the day itself. Two things change, and they are the whole argument.
The accent moves to Count the till — the one thing standing between this day and being closed.
And the comparison stops pretending: today is measured against where a typical Tuesday stood AT 16:52, not against a whole one. An unfinished day beside a finished one reads as a bad day every single afternoon.

The day sheet. A4 at 96px per inch, one page, 12pt floor on every reading line.
It carries its own provenance — what was summarised rather than listed, and when it was printed — because this is the copy that gets handed to somebody who is arguing about a Tuesday.

A quiet day, a day that has not happened, too few Tuesdays to compare against, and the drawer disagreeing with the book.
The last one is a state the current screen cannot show at all: it never reads the count.
At the foot, every removal, and the four things this deliberately does not touch.
